questions.q: What does RPO (Recovery Point Objective) actually measure?
options: How long the system can be down after a disaster
The maximum acceptable amount of data loss, measured in time
The cost of running a disaster recovery drill
How many backups exist in storage
questions.explain: RPO answers 'how far back could the restored data be, worst case' — a measure of acceptable data loss, not downtime.

questions.q: What does RTO (Recovery Time Objective) actually measure?
options: The maximum acceptable amount of data loss
The maximum acceptable time to get the system back up and serving requests after a disaster is declared
The number of regions a database is replicated to
The backup file's compression ratio
questions.explain: RTO measures downtime — how long from disaster declared to service restored — a different axis from RPO's data-loss measurement.

questions.q: What RPO and RTO targets does this capstone set for Overlook's database, and why?
options: RPO of 24 hours and RTO of 1 week, because healthcare data isn't time-sensitive
RPO of 5 minutes and RTO of 1 hour, because appointment and billing writes are business-critical and extended downtime has real operational and reputational cost
No specific targets are set; 'as soon as possible' is the plan
RPO of 0 and RTO of 0, which is always achievable for any database
questions.explain: These are deliberate, board-level targets worked backward from an acceptable worst case, not arbitrary round numbers.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say 'we have backups' was never a real disaster recovery plan for Overlook?
options: Because backups don't actually protect any data
Because a backup existing somewhere is not the same as a tested, targeted recovery plan with concrete RPO/RTO numbers
Because Overlook never actually had working backups
Because backups are only useful for performance tuning
questions.explain: The Beginner capstone built real backups, but backups alone don't define or test how much loss or downtime is acceptable — that's what RPO/RTO planning adds.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say these RPO/RTO numbers matter differently for Overlook than for a typical retail database?
options: They don't matter differently — all databases have identical risk profiles
Losing appointment and billing writes risks patients with appointments that no longer exist and billing records that don't match what actually happened, a different category of consequence
Healthcare databases are always smaller, so recovery is faster automatically
Retail databases never need disaster recovery plans
questions.explain: The consequences of data loss or downtime are directly patient-facing, which is why the board's mandate called this out specifically.
